extracted.intended_audience: Lincoln scholars, historians, students of 19th-century education, and general readers interested in Abraham Lincoln's early life and mathematical training
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating documentary and testimonial evidence (copybook pages, textbooks, witness statements, provenance) to judge Abraham Lincoln's level and sequence of mathematical study during his Indiana years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the arithmetic copybook as documentary proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Young Lincoln's 'arithmetical copy-book' or 'Book of Examples in Arithmetic' provides documentary evidence regarding his attainments as a student in Indiana (e.g., sheets dated March 1, 1826, headed 'Discount').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give high weight to dated, worked pages from Lincoln's own hand; specific dated pages (such as March 1, 1826, 'Discount') indicate topics studied and can be used to infer progression and competence. Note that only a fraction of the original (~10–12 sheets surviving of ~100) remain, so conclusions must account for missing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of copybook content with contemporary textbooks (Pike's, Daboll's)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare problems, captions, definitions, and topic order in the copybook with Pike's Arithmetic and Daboll's Arithmetic to identify sources and map Lincoln's sequence of study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use textbook page ranges (e.g., Pike: 'Multiplication' pages 13–17; 'Rule of Three' pages 100–130; 'Discount' page 220; 'Compound Interest' near end) to infer how far Lincoln had progressed and when he studied particular topics. Note Dr. Warren's observation that the copybook shows Pike's and Daboll's influence though not verbatim copying, implying teacher-arranged exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic coverage as indicator of mathematical level
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific subjects present in the copybook (multiplication, compound multiplication, rule of three/proportion, simple and compound interest, discount, examples in compound interest) indicate the complexity reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If copybook pages include higher topics such as 'Discount' and 'Compound Interest' one can infer completion of over two-thirds of a standard arithmetic text and thus collegiate-equivalent arithmetic training for that era. Presence of surveying, geometry, and trigonometry material further indicates practical higher mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological inference from textbook order and dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the order of subjects in standard textbooks and dates on copybook pages to place Lincoln's mathematical progress in time (e.g., he studied 'Multiplication' in 1824 and 'Discount' on March 1, 1826).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map dated copybook entries to textbook sequencing to estimate age at mastery of topics (example: mastering 'Rule of Three' sometime before March 1826 implies competence by ~16–17 years). Treat such inferences as approximate and contingent on the assumption Lincoln followed typical topic order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and custodial history of surviving sheets
rubrics_metrics.description: Trace who collected, preserved, and later possessed the copybook sheets (Mrs. Lincoln → Herndon → Weik → scattered recipients; reports of missing pages sold by Thomas Johnson) to establish authenticity and completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate credibility based on chain-of-custody, existence of photostats, and institutional holdings (Barrett collection, Brown University, Chicago Historical Society, Lincoln National Life Foundation). Scattered or lost leaves reduce completeness and require cautious interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handwriting, presentation, and methods shown on pages
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of Lincoln's handwriting, the use of captions (e.g., 'The Single Rule of Three'), proofs (answers proven by division or addition), and careful printed headings ('Abraham Lincoln His Book') reflect the student's skill and thoroughness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess neatness, organization, presence of definitions/rules, and checking methods as evidence of competent, methodical study. Contemporary observers (e.g., Arnold) considered Lincoln's specimen unusually well-written for a 17-year-old, which strengthens inferences about ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership/inscription in textbooks as evidence of study (e.g., Gibson's surveying)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of Lincoln's name or marginalia in subject books (for example, 'The Theory and Practice of Surveying' by Robert Gibson) supports claims he studied surveying and related geometry/trigonometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inscriptions and ownership marks in extant books as corroborating evidence that Lincoln consulted or learned from those texts; cross-check with copybook content and accounts of tutoring (e.g., James Blair, Reuben Grigsby lending books).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and reliability of contemporary testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Use statements by contemporaries (Herndon, Arnold, Matilda Johnson, Nathaniel Grigsby, Elias Mason, Ann (Kate) Roby) to supplement documentary evidence, but assess each witness's reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat testimony differently depending on source: professional friends and those with direct access to manuscripts (Arnold, Herndon) are valuable, but some informants (e.g., Dennis Hanks) are described as 'a rich mine of misinformation.' Corroborate oral accounts with documentary materials when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about autobiographical and rhetorical self-presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lincoln's own campaign autobiographies (1859–60) understate his education (phrases like 'literally without education', 'did not know much') and were used for political advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider motive and context when using autobiographical statements as evidence; such self-portrayals may be deliberate understatements and should be balanced against contemporaneous documentary evidence and external testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context of local educational resources (subscription schools, teachers, textbooks circulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the educational environment: subscription schools of ~3 months' term, often minimal facilities; teachers often of meager qualifications; community circulation of academic textbooks among settlers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the likelihood Lincoln had access to advanced texts and tutors by noting neighbors who attended higher schools, availability of borrowed textbooks, and the common practice of 'books brought home and passed around.' This contextual evidence supports or limits conclusions about self-study opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pedagogical signs such as exercises arranged by teacher
rubrics_metrics.description: The copybook appears to be an 'exercise book' with examples 'arranged and presented by the teacher' rather than verbatim copies of textbook illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret structure and phrasing (definitions followed by rules and proofs) as evidence of formal instruction or guided practice; where content mirrors textbook topics but not exact wording, infer teacher-mediated exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-referencing with published Lincoln scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Corroborate findings with prior scholarship (Tarbell, Barton, Warren, the Southwestern Indiana Historical Society, Murr, Vannest, Ehrmann) and with journal publications like 'Lincoln Lore'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent scholarly studies and published reproductions of copybook pages to validate provenance, dating, and interpretations. Consider consensus and dissent among historians when weighing conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat for missing/lost evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that the loss of Lincoln's literary copybook and many arithmetic pages limits the available documentary record and constrains definitive conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where evidence is absent, avoid overclaiming; treat conclusions as probabilistic and conditioned on surviving material. Note traditions about missing leaves (sold individually) and explicitly state uncertainty when reconstructing full curriculum or degree-equivalent education.
